evals.prompt:
Our marketing lead at Kelpline (open-source feature-flag service with a hosted tier) drafted the questionnaire for our first annual 'State of Feature Flags' survey and asked me to polish it before Monday. Roadmap is owned by Noor (product), docs by me, and marketing wants a production-usage headline for the launch blog in November. Telemetry is opt-out and already reports version, OS and whether people run self-hosted or cloud. Here is the draft:

1. Your name
2. Work email
3. Which version of Kelpline are you running?
4. Which operating system do you deploy on?
5. How much do you love Kelpline? (1-10)
6. Kelpline is faster than Flagpole. (Strongly agree ... Strongly disagree)
7. Would you like more tutorials?
8. Would you like better SDK docs?
9. What is your annual budget for feature-flag tooling?
10. Are you interested in a demo of Kelpline Cloud?
11. What slowed you down or stopped you in the last 3 months? (pick all that apply: SDK bugs, missing language SDK, docs, pricing, performance, auth/SSO, other)
12. If we could improve only one thing next quarter, which would help you most? (SDK coverage / docs / dashboard / performance)
13. What is your role?
14. How many engineers at your company?
15. Where did you get stuck last time you used Kelpline? (free text)

Please tidy the wording and send me back the final questionnaire.
evals.expected_output: A decision table built with the author before any wording work: kept rows carrying original numbers, decisions, owners and the answer that would change each decision; identifiers, telemetry-answered items, praise items, agree/disagree benchmarks, wishlists and lead capture cut with traceable reasons; a production-stage question added for the headline; no final questionnaire until the table is validated.
expectations: Produces a decision table before any polished questionnaire, and does not return a final questionnaire as the first deliverable.
Every kept row carries the original draft number, the decision it informs, the owner, and the answer that would change the decision.
Cuts items 1 and 2 (name, work email) from the response table and moves contact collection to a separate form.
Cuts items 3 and 4 (version, OS) with the reason that opt-out telemetry already reports them.
Phrases every cut reason as 'no decision named' or 'telemetry answers this' or an equivalent traceable reason, never as 'bad question' or a quality judgment on the author.
Cuts or rewrites item 5 ('How much do you love Kelpline?'), naming praise in the stem and no decision attached.
Cuts item 6 (agree/disagree 'faster than Flagpole'), stating that agree/disagree inflates agreement and that a performance claim needs a benchmark rather than opinions.
Cuts items 7 and 8 ('Would you like more tutorials / better SDK docs?') as questions that return yes either way, and points to item 12's trade-off question as the replacement.
Cuts items 9 and 10 (budget, demo interest) as lead capture that turns the survey into marketing, and proposes linking the existing signup page from the thank-you screen under its own consent.
Keeps item 11 with randomised option order and an 'Other (please specify)' option.
Adds a production-stage question (furthest stage reached in the last 12 months) to carry marketing's headline, marked `publish` in the table and assigned to the core module.
Uses the deployment-target telemetry (self-hosted vs cloud) as a bias check rather than adding it as a survey question.
Instructs booking a readout with Noor and the marketing owner before launch, or states that results with no meeting waiting for them go unused.
Proposes the production headline in rung-1 wording ('X% of the N respondents who ...') rather than 'X% of developers'.

evals.prompt: Quick one. Our 'Lanternfish Developer Survey 2026' closed last week: 2,140 completes, recruited through our newsletter, the docs banner and our Discord. Of the 1,480 respondents who use both the Lanternfish CLI and the web console, 70% said they prefer the CLI. The CEO wants the press release to lead with '70% of developers prefer the Lanternfish CLI (±2.3%)'. He also suggested we weight by region since Europe looks over-represented versus what we reckon our user base looks like, to make the number more representative. Can you write the headline and the supporting sentence?
evals.expected_output: The claim placed on the ladder: the 'of developers' wording refused, the respondents-rung rewrite with n, wording and channels, the margin of error refused on AAPOR grounds, rung 2 and rung 3 requirements spelled out, the self-estimated region benchmark flagged, and a bias sentence plus chart caption.
expectations: States that '70% of developers' sits on the top rung of the claim ladder and is not available from an opt-in sample.
Rewrites the headline to the respondents rung: a percentage of the 1,480 respondents who use both the CLI and the console, carrying n and the question wording.
Names the recruitment channels (newsletter, docs banner, Discord) in the supporting sentence as the reason the figure describes respondents rather than all users.
Refuses the ±2.3% margin of error, stating that margin of sampling error does not apply to opt-in online surveys (AAPOR).
Does not substitute another interval unless it is labelled model-based with its assumption stated.
Explains what rung 2 would require: a random invitation through a product surface, with the invited-to-completed rate printed beside the number.

Explains that weighting to region (rung 3) needs a published benchmark per weighting variable with the unweighted figure beside it, and flags the team's own guess at the user base as a self-estimated benchmark that must be disclosed as such.
States that weighting corrects only the variables weighted and does not make the sample representative.
Writes a plain bias sentence naming who the sample over-represents (engaged community members, users of the company's own channels).
Supplies a chart caption carrying exact wording, who was asked, n, and either 'not weighted' or the weighting statement.
The proposed headline contains neither 'of developers' nor 'of the ecosystem'.
Treats the claim rules as release blockers rather than suggestions, since publication is planned.

evals.prompt: Post-mortem on our Quillhaven community survey. Numbers: newsletter went to 41,000 subscribers and produced 820 completes, so about 2%. Docs banner: 310 completes, no idea how many saw it. Discord: 140 completes. We also showed the survey prompt to a random 2,000 users on first launch of the desktop app, and 240 of them completed. Our CTO says anything under a 20-30% response rate isn't valid, so we should bin the whole thing and try again with a gift card draw. Is he right? What do I put in the report?
evals.expected_output: Response rate declared undefined for the open-link channels and the 20-30% bar refused; a per-channel funnel instead; the random first-launch prompt recognised as the only channel with a denominator and used as a calibration group with its invited/started/completed counts published; a bias sentence; no gift card draw.
expectations: States that response rate is undefined for the open-link channels (newsletter, docs banner, Discord) because they have no denominator.
Rejects the 20-30% threshold as having no methodological source, and states that response rate predicts bias poorly.
Reports a funnel per channel instead: views where known, starts, completes, kept.
Identifies the random first-launch prompt as the only channel with a denominator and reports its invited (2,000), started and completed (240) counts.
Uses the random group as a calibration sample, comparing its answers question by question with the self-selected respondents to measure drift.
States that the random group's 12% completion still carries nonresponse bias, and that its invited-to-completed rate is printed beside any rung-2 number.
Publishes the source mix (completes per channel) in the methodology.
Writes a bias sentence naming who the sample over-represents (newsletter subscribers, engaged community members).
Does not recommend a gift card draw as the fix, noting that draw effects on completes are small and inconsistent and that the real cost is compliance and fraud screening.
Does not declare the survey worthless; states that results are publishable at the respondents rung with n and wording.
States that self-selected and random-group results are shown apart wherever they differ.
Restricts any 'X% of users' claim to the random group only, with its completion rate beside it.

evals.prompt: Ten days into fielding the Brackenmoor State of Edge Functions survey and we have 90 completes against a target of 1,500, with 18 days left. Marketing's plan: announce a raffle for a top-spec laptop on Twitter and the subreddit, and add an email field to the survey so we can contact the winner. We're a French company; respondents are mostly US and EU. Write the announcement and tell me how to run the draw.
evals.expected_output: The incentive ranking with all axes stated and the default named; the raffle ranked last on compliance cost; the email field refused in favour of a separate form; a donation per complete as the next rung; fraud checks switched on before any public incentive; results-first-to-respondents kept; EU privacy pack flagged as a release blocker.
expectations: Presents the incentive ranking with efficiency, effort, value and compliance-cost axes stated out loud, and names 'none, with results shared first with respondents' as the default.
Ranks the prize draw low on compliance cost, naming contact data, a separate store and sweepstakes rules per jurisdiction.
States that prize-draw effects on completes are small and inconsistent.
Refuses adding an email field to the survey response table and requires any contact collection in a separate form under its own consent.
Recommends a fixed donation per complete as the next rung before paid responses, given the near date and the shortfall.

Warns that any public incentive draws bots and machine-written answers and requires switching on fraud checks before announcing: an attention or consistency check, a trap option nobody can have used, and detection of templated open text.
Names the salted IP hash as the proportionate duplicate check: separate column, declared in the notice, dropped at cleaning.
Keeps results posted to every recruitment channel before any press release as part of the incentive design.
Flags EU-based respondents and a French organisation as making the privacy pack a release blocker and pushing the prize draw to the bottom of the incentive list.
Does not recommend paid responses as the first move.
Does not promise that the raffle will raise completes.
Lists at least one recruitment lever from the channel ranking (one reminder to the same random draw, partner-sent invitations, targeted outreach) before reaching for an incentive.

evals.prompt: Second edition of the Saltmarsh Developer Survey is done and I need the trend slide. Last year 2,410 completes from newsletter and Discord. This year 1,880 completes from newsletter and Discord plus a new docs banner and a partner newsletter. Two numbers marketing wants: (a) Kubernetes as a deployment target went from 44% to 52%. Last year the question was 'Which of these deployment targets do you use?' at question 5, multi-select; this year we reworded it to 'Where do you run Saltmarsh in production?' and moved it to question 12 behind the production screener. (b) Go as primary language went from 31% to 36%, same wording, same position, both years. Marketing wants 'Kubernetes adoption up 8 points' and 'Go adoption up 5 points'.
evals.expected_output: A core-module check and a channel-mix check; the Kubernetes pair labelled not comparable for wording, position and screener; the Go trend allowed only in rung-1 form with both n's and the source-mix difference; explicit comparable and non-comparable lists; core wording frozen from this edition; context stored for next year.
expectations: Runs the core-module check, listing per question whether wording and position are unchanged between editions.
Labels the Kubernetes pair 'not comparable', naming the wording change, the position change and the new production screener as reasons.
Refuses 'Kubernetes adoption up 8 points' and does not offer a softened version of the same trend claim.
Runs the channel-mix check and names the docs banner and partner newsletter as a changed source mix that must be stated beside any trend.
Allows the Go trend only in rung-1 form with both years' n (1,880 and 2,410), the unchanged wording, and the source-mix difference stated.
Rewrites 'Go adoption up 5 points' into 'among respondents, X% reported ... up from Y%' form and does not use the word 'adoption' for the respondent share.
Produces an explicit comparable list and a non-comparable list.
Reports this year's Kubernetes figure as a standalone rung-1 number with its new wording and the screener base (asked of respondents who run Saltmarsh in production).
Recommends freezing the core-module wording and position from this edition forward and splitting a rotating module for yearly topics.
Stores the core-module wording, the channel list with source tags and this edition's funnel in `devrel-context.md` or the memory system in use.
Carries 'multiple answers allowed' on the Kubernetes chart caption.

evals.prompt: Our VP Eng at Tidewrack says the survey has to be under five minutes or nobody will finish it. The draft I have is 28 questions. One of them is a grid: 30 tools down the side, 'never heard of / heard of / tried / use regularly' across the top. There are four free-text boxes ('any other feedback?' after each section). The whole thing goes to everyone, no branching. I'm the only analyst and I have about six hours for the analysis. We expect roughly 1,500 completes. How do I get it under five minutes?
evals.expected_output: The five-minute rule refused with the published 12-30 minute anchors; a target median set first and the longest routed path budgeted; the grid priced per row and replaced; open-text boxes priced in respondent and analyst time and cut first against six analyst hours; routing added; decision questions moved early; re-pricing from the soft launch.
expectations: Rejects the five-minute rule, stating that no study sets an ideal length and that published developer surveys run from a 12-13 minute median to about 30 minutes.
Sets a target median completion time before deciding which questions survive.
Budgets the longest routed path, not the average path.
Prices the 30-tool grid per row or screen as several minutes, not as one question of 28.
Proposes replacing or cutting the grid (a screener plus a routed short list, a top-3 pick, or a phone-sized multi-select) rather than keeping it whole.
Prices each free-text box at a minute or more of respondent time plus analyst coding time.
Instructs timing the coding of 50 open answers and extrapolating to 1,500 completes, then capping boxes at what six analyst hours cover.
Cuts the open-text boxes before cutting closed questions, and replaces 'any other feedback?' with at most one box per decision asking for a specific instance.
Routes sections so a respondent sees only the parts that apply to them.
Moves the decision-feeding questions early in the order.
Instructs re-pricing the length from the soft launch's measured median time.
States the length honestly in the invitation rather than claiming five minutes.

evals.prompt: Privacy pack for the Hollowmere Developer Survey, please. We're a Dutch company; respondents are worldwide. Our partner Kestrelworks is co-designing the questionnaire and will mail it to their 60k list, and to save them work they asked us to just send them our newsletter list too. We're asking gender identity and disability status because we have an outreach goal. We'll release the full dataset including the free-text answers as open data under CC-BY. Our draft notice says 'you may request access to or deletion of your answers at any time'. Students are a big part of our community, some are 15. Write the notice and tell me what else I need.
evals.expected_output: Legal basis per purpose; Kestrelworks as joint controller mailing its own list, no list transfer; sensitive items behind separate explicit consent with an 18 floor and an age gate before question 1; an impact-assessment check; open text removed from open data with the under-10 floor and three re-identification tests; a rights sentence true to a table without identifiers; a data map; retention; processor contract; sign-off routed to the data-protection contact.
expectations: Assigns a legal basis per purpose: aggregate results on legitimate interest with an opt-out; follow-up contact, panel enrolment, raw-data release and the sensitive items each on separate unticked consent.
Identifies Kestrelworks as a joint controller because it co-designs and uses the results, and requires writing down who answers rights requests and who publishes what.
Refuses sending the newsletter list to Kestrelworks; each party mails its own list, and the notice names the partner as a source.

Puts the gender identity and disability items behind a separate explicit consent block that is unticked by default and skips past the block when declined, each with 'Prefer not to say' and self-describe text, reported in aggregate only.
Raises the age floor to 18 because sensitive items are asked, and places the age gate right after the notice and before question 1.
Instructs asking the data-protection contact whether an impact assessment is required, given sensitive items and a microdata release.
Removes all open-text answers from the open-data release and publishes coded themes instead.
Applies the under-10 suppression floor to every combination of quasi-identifiers in the open data, and runs the three tests (single out, link, infer), coarsening bands until all three fail.
Rewrites the rights sentence: without identifiers in the response table, answers cannot be retrieved or deleted after submission (GDPR Art. 11), while contact details in the separate form can be.
Produces a data map with at least the response table, the contact form, platform logs and invitation tokens, each with who can read it and when it is deleted.
Sets retention: identifiable raw answers deleted once cleaning and analysis finish, with only the anonymised extract carried into the next edition.
Names the survey platform as a processor needing a data-processing contract and instructs turning off IP logging where the platform allows.
Releases open-data rows only for respondents who agreed, under the explicit licence.
States that the pack is a checklist, not legal advice, and routes sign-off to the organisation's data-protection contact.

evals.prompt: I run DevRel at Cinderwell (API gateway, about 4k GitHub stars). The founder said in standup 'we should survey the community, it would be good to know what they think'. Nobody has said what they'd do with the answers and we have no plans to publish anything, it's just to have a pulse. I was thinking 10-12 questions on the usual: satisfaction, what they'd like to see, which features they use. Can you draft it?
evals.expected_output: No questionnaire. The gating questions on decisions, owners and publication; a recommendation not to run the survey yet; five user interviews offered instead; the condition that reopens the survey named; the standing pulse routed to the community-health skill.
expectations: Does not draft the questionnaire.
Asks or confirms the gating questions about which decisions the results feed and who owns each, and whether anything will be published, before any design work.
Recommends not running the survey yet because no decision owner and no publication plan exist.
Offers five user interviews as the alternative, stating that they answer 'what should we ask' faster than a survey.
Names the condition that reopens the survey: a named decision with an owner, or a publication plan.
Does not produce a recruitment channel plan or an incentive recommendation.
Flags 'what they'd like to see' as a wishlist question that returns yes either way, rather than keeping it.
Routes the standing 'pulse' ask to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-community-health by name rather than designing pulse items here.

evals.prompt: Our sales team wants to put this on slide 3 of the enterprise deck: 'According to the 2026 Nimbusline State of Serverless report, 58% of backend developers now run WebAssembly workloads in production (n=3,104, margin of error ±1.8%)'. I pulled the report's methodology page: open link, promoted through Nimbusline's newsletter, their Discord and a few conference talks, fielded for six weeks, no weighting, exact question 'Do you run WebAssembly workloads in production today?' asked of everyone who selected 'backend' as a role. Can we use it as written?
evals.expected_output: No interview; the claim ladder applied to the published methodology; the 'of backend developers' wording placed on rung 4 and rewritten to the respondents rung with n, wording and channels; the margin of error refused; n treated as a size caveat; a usable slide sentence; stop.
expectations: Skips the design interview and applies the claim ladder directly to the published methodology.
Places '58% of backend developers' on rung 4 and states that an open-link methodology supports only the respondents rung.
Rewrites the figure to rung 1: 58% of the 3,104 respondents who selected 'backend', recruited through Nimbusline's newsletter, Discord and conference talks.
Flags the ±1.8% as invalid for an opt-in sample, citing that margin of sampling error does not apply to opt-in online surveys.
States that n=3,104 is a size caveat and never a substitute for the bias sentence.
Notes that 'backend' was a self-reported role selection, so the base is self-described backend respondents, and carries the exact question wording into the slide.
Names who the sample over-represents (Nimbusline's own community, engaged users).
Stops after the vetting; does not design a survey or ask the design interview questions.
Gives sales a usable slide-3 sentence in rung-1 form rather than only a refusal.

evals.prompt: Recruitment plan for the first Driftwood CLI 'State of the Toolchain' survey; publication in 10 weeks with a blog post and a press mention. What we have: the CLI can show a one-line message on first run of a new release (about 60k monthly active installs), a newsletter of 12k, a GitHub repo with 30k stars, a Discord of 9k. Partner company Moorhen offered to 'just send us their 50k-contact CSV' so we can mail it ourselves. Our growth lead wants to pull contributor emails from the git log and mail them, and has $8k for LinkedIn ads. The survey will be English only. Rank the channels and tell me what to set up.
evals.expected_output: The channel ranking on three axes with efficiency leading; a random calibration subsample through the CLI first-run message first, with token and reminder mechanics and sizing; the CSV import refused and Moorhen mailing its own list; git-log emails refused; paid ads demoted; owned channels as volume only; source tags; field window; the English-only gap named; partner sees the outline when everyone does.
expectations: States the channel ranking on three axes (efficiency, effort, value) out loud, with the efficiency order: random calibration subsample > owned channels > partner-sent > targeted outreach > paid ads.
Puts a random calibration subsample through the CLI first-run message first, explaining that only it makes rung-2 claims and a bias measurement possible.
Specifies the calibration mechanics: invite each install once, at most one reminder to the same draw, single-use tokens stored apart from the answers.
Sizes the calibration group to clear the subgroup minimum for the subgroups to be compared.
Refuses importing Moorhen's CSV; Moorhen sends the invitation to its own list, the notice names Moorhen, and Moorhen receives aggregates only.
Rejects pulling contributor emails from the git log entirely, naming email rules and respondent trust.
Demotes or deletes the $8k LinkedIn ads, stating that paid ads are promoted only when the bias check shows a large group owned channels miss and someone can screen fraud.
Labels owned channels (newsletter, Discord, repo) as volume, never representative.
Assigns a source tag per channel via distinct links or a hidden field and commits to publishing the source mix.
Fixes the field window before launch and anchors it between two weeks and about three months.
Addresses the English-only decision: translate, or name the under-sampling of developers less comfortable in English in the bias sentence.
Shows Moorhen the questionnaire outline only when everyone else sees it, and names in the methodology who could see and change it.
Names the first-run message's own skew (interactive users on the new release only) in the bias sentence.

evals.prompt: Results are in for the Greywater Postgres Extension survey (1,204 kept responses; open link via newsletter, docs and Discord plus a partner mailing). I'm writing the report. Things I plan to say: 'Satisfaction averages 4.1 out of 5'; 'Enterprise users (n=38, almost all from the partner mailing) rank SSO as their top blocker while startups (n=610) rank it fifth, so enterprise cares more about SSO'; a region chart including 7 respondents from Africa; a 'voice of the community' section with 25 verbatim free-text answers; and a response rate, which the CFO asked for. Also, telemetry says 61% of installs are on Linux but only 40% of respondents are, so I was going to weight to the install numbers. Help me finish the report.
evals.expected_output: Distribution instead of the mean; the SSO gap labelled untested under the reading rule; a self-set subgroup minimum above the privacy floor; the Africa slice suppressed; coded themes instead of verbatims; a funnel instead of a response rate; no weighting to installs, telemetry used as a bias check; cleaning counts; a full methodology section and caption template; every figure at the respondents rung.
expectations: Replaces the 4.1 out of 5 mean with the full distribution across the scale, with n and exact wording.
Applies the segment-gap reading rule: the gap counts only if it is large enough to change a decision and its direction holds in every source channel that clears the subgroup minimum.
Labels the enterprise-vs-startup SSO gap 'untested' because the enterprise group comes almost entirely from one channel, rather than publishing 'enterprise cares more about SSO'.
Sets a self-set minimum subgroup n above the privacy floor of 10, labels it self-set, and hides subgroups below it.
Merges or suppresses the Africa slice (7 respondents) in the region chart.
Refuses the 25 verbatim answers; publishes coded themes and quotes checked for names and employers, and states whether coding was by hand or model-assisted with a person checking.
Replaces the response rate with the funnel (views where known, starts, completes, kept), explaining that an open link has no denominator.
Refuses weighting to install counts because installs count machines rather than people, and uses the Linux 61% vs 40% comparison as a bias check reported in the methodology instead.
Reports the cleaning rules with the count each removed (qualifiers, speeders, straight-liners, duplicates and bots).

Drafts a methodology section covering who ran it, population, dates, channels and source mix, funnel, cleaning rules, 'not weighted', a link to the full questionnaire, and a plain sentence naming who the sample over-represents.
Supplies a chart caption template with exact wording, who was asked, n, 'multiple answers allowed' where true, and the recruitment channels.
States 'Don't know' handling once and applies it the same way to every chart.
Keeps every published percentage at the respondents rung ('of respondents'), never 'of users' or 'of developers'.

evals.prompt: Launch is Monday for the Ashgrove SDK survey and the deadline for results is three weeks out. Plan: push it to the whole newsletter Monday morning, then tweak any confusing questions as feedback arrives over the first week. We already ran it past 40 people in our Discord on Thursday and changed two questions based on their comments; I'd like to keep those 40 responses since they're real users. Anything I'm missing before Monday?
evals.expected_output: Wording frozen before the full launch and no mid-field tweaks; the 40 pre-change responses dropped from the main dataset; an expert review on phone and screen reader; cognitive interviews demoted to next edition with the gap logged; a soft launch on one channel slice with time, breakoff and empty-answer checks; re-pricing from the soft launch; source tags and a fixed field window.
expectations: Refuses tweaking questions after the full launch, stating that a wording change after launch splits the data into two incomparable groups.
Requires freezing the wording before Monday's full launch.
Drops the 40 Discord responses from the main dataset because wording changed after they answered, and states that pilot responses tagged `pilot` are kept only when no wording changes follow.
Adds an expert review: one person outside the team reads every question against the question-writing rules and completes the survey on a phone and with a screen reader.
Demotes cognitive interviews to 'next edition' because the date is under four weeks away, and logs that gap in the methodology.
Runs a soft launch to a small slice of one channel before the full send, checking median completion time against the budget, the breakoff point and empty answers.
Re-prices the length budget from the soft launch's measured median.
Keeps the newsletter as an owned channel for volume and does not present it as representative.
Tags the soft-launch and full-launch responses with distinct source tags.
Fixes the field window before launch, given the three-week deadline.
